exam_points: Neuron-to-neuron signalling is electrical → chemical → electrical.
Ca²⁺ entry through presynaptic voltage-gated channels triggers exocytosis.
Six events: AP, Ca²⁺ entry, release, receptor binding, ions enter, graded potential.
EPSP: positive ions in (Na⁺). IPSP: negative ions in (Cl⁻), hyperpolarizes.
Rest -70 mV, threshold -50 to -55 mV, PSP about ±10 mV: one EPSP is not enough.
Temporal summation: one neuron, rapid firing. Spatial: many neurons at once.
Glutamate main excitatory; GABA (and glycine) main inhibitory.
ACh: nicotinic excitatory at the NMJ; muscarinic inhibitory in the heart.
Direct (ionotropic) = fast; indirect (second messenger, cAMP) = slow, long-lasting.
Signal ends by reuptake, enzymes (AChE: acetate + choline) and diffusion.
SSRIs block serotonin reuptake; tetanus toxin blocks GABA release.

Sensitization: serotonin → cAMP → K⁺ channels blocked → longer AP → more release.
Pain and temperature cross in the cord; fine touch and vibration in the medulla.

deeper.title: Electrical versus chemical synapses
deeper.html:
Electrical synapses link cells through gap junctions, so current flows straight from one cell to the next with almost no delay and in both directions. That suits cells that must fire together, such as cardiac muscle and some smooth muscle. Chemical synapses are slower (a fraction of a millisecond of synaptic delay) and one-way, but the transmitter step lets the signal be amplified, inhibited, summed and changed by drugs. That flexibility is why almost all CNS signalling, and all of pharmacology at the synapse, is chemical.

Standard comparison, added to cover the lecture's learning objective.

deeper.title: Why one EPSP is never enough
deeper.html:
The lecture's numbers make the point: a neuron rests at -70 mV, fires at about -50 to -55 mV, and a single PSP moves it by about 10 mV. A neuron is therefore a counter, not a relay. It adds the EPSPs and IPSPs arriving from thousands of synapses (convergence) at the axon hillock, and fires only when excitation wins. This is what lets the nervous system make decisions rather than just pass messages on.

Source: the lecture's summation slides.

deeper.title: Sensitization and pain
deeper.html:
The sensitization mechanism in the lecture is the cellular basis of why a burned or bruised area hurts more on the next touch. Serotonin released after the injury blocks presynaptic K⁺ channels through cAMP, so each action potential lasts longer, lets in more Ca²⁺ and releases more transmitter. The same input now produces a bigger output.

Source: the lecture's neuron sensitization slide.

deeper.title: Why touch soothes pain
deeper.html:
Rubbing a bumped elbow works because of the gate theory: the A-beta touch fibres activate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that damp the C-fibre pain signal before it ascends. It is also the idea behind TENS machines.

Source: the lecture's gate theory slide.

deeper.title: Why atropine dries the mouth
deeper.html:
Saliva is driven by parasympathetic ACh on muscarinic receptors. Block those receptors and secretion stops, while the ganglia, which use nicotinic receptors, are unaffected. The receptor split in this lecture explains why drugs can target one division or organ.

Source: the lecture's receptor and synapse slides.

exam_points: Muscle only pulls: force by shortening, never by pushing.
Skeletal: multinucleate, peripheral nuclei, striated, voluntary, Ca²⁺ from SR, troponin.
Smooth: one central nucleus, no sarcomeres, calmodulin, slowest myosin ATPase.
Cardiac: striated, involuntary, intercalated discs with gap junctions, pacemaker.
Five properties: contractility, conductivity, excitability, extensibility, elasticity.
Triad = one T-tubule + two terminal cisternae of the SR.
Fibre number fixed at birth; training causes hypertrophy.
Myosin hexamer: 2 heavy + 4 light chains; head has the ATP and actin sites.
Z (between), I (isotropic, thin only), A (anisotropic, thick length), H (helles, thick only), M (middle).
Thin 8 nm, thick 16 nm, about 2 thin per thick.
DHP receptor (T-tubule Ca²⁺ channel) gates the ryanodine receptor (SR); SERCA pumps Ca²⁺ back.
Sliding: filaments keep their length; A band constant; I band and H zone shorten.
Isotonic shortens; isometric develops tension without shortening.

deeper.title: Why the A band never changes
deeper.html:
The A band is defined by the thick filaments, and myosin filaments do not change length. When the muscle contracts, the thin filaments slide in from both sides, so the light zones that contain only one type of filament (the I band with actin only, the H zone with myosin only) get smaller, while the dark A band stays exactly as wide. Ask yourself which filament defines each band and the answer to any 'what shortens' question follows.

Source: the lecture's sliding filament slides.

deeper.title: Calcium tells you the muscle type
deeper.html:
Skeletal muscle keeps all its trigger Ca²⁺ in the SR and reads it with troponin, which makes it fast and tightly controlled by nerves. Smooth muscle also uses extracellular Ca²⁺ and reads it with calmodulin through a slower enzyme cascade, which suits slow, sustained tone in vessel and gut walls. Cardiac muscle sits in between. Most comparison questions in this lecture can be answered from this one difference.

Source: the lecture's comparison table of skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Covasa's lecture: the neuromuscular junction, excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle, muscle energetics, tension and motor units, fibre types and training, fatigue and rigor mortis, and the diseases of the neuromuscular system. Several slides in the PDF are images only, so their content is not covered here. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Motor unit: one motor neuron and all its fibres; each fibre has one neuron.
NMJ: vesicles of about 1000 ACh; cleft about 50 nm; nicotinic receptors on the end plate.
Ca2+ entry at the terminal triggers ACh release; AChE ends the signal.
Nicotinic receptor: ligand-gated cation channel, two ACh on two α subunits.
mEPP about 0.5 mV; EPP about 50 mV from about 100 vesicles.
EC coupling: T-tubule, DHP receptor, ryanodine receptor, Ca2+ binds troponin, SERCA returns Ca2+.
Smooth muscle uses calmodulin and MLCK; nitric oxide relaxes it.
ATP stores last about 8 twitches; creatine kinase buffers.
Resting sarcomere length 75 to 130 percent of optimal.
Force is graded by recruitment and frequency.
Type I slow oxidative red; IIb fast glycolytic white.
Fatigue at about 30 percent ATP depletion; rigor mortis at 100 percent.
McArdle: no phosphorylase, second wind. Tarui: no PFK.
Myasthenia gravis: postsynaptic receptors. Lambert-Eaton: presynaptic Ca2+ channels.
Duchenne: X-linked dystrophin loss, raised CK.

deeper.title: Why myasthenia gets worse through the day
deeper.html:
In myasthenia gravis there are fewer working ACh receptors, so each nerve impulse produces a smaller end plate potential. Early on, enough ACh is released to reach threshold, but with repeated use the ACh release per impulse falls, and the smaller EPPs start to miss threshold. That is why weakness, often of the eyelids, worsens with use and through the day, and why AChE inhibitors help: they leave more ACh in the cleft.

Source: the lecture's NMJ and myasthenic disease slides.

deeper.title: Why low calcium causes muscle spasms
deeper.html:
The lecture lists hypocalcaemic tetany. Low extracellular Ca2+ makes nerve membranes more excitable, so they fire on their own and the muscles they supply contract repeatedly. It explains the tingling and hand spasms after thyroid or parathyroid surgery, linking this lecture to the thyroid anatomy you learned.

Source: the lecture's hypocalcaemic tetany slide.

deeper.title: Why rigor mortis starts and then fades
deeper.html:
After death, ATP runs out, and without ATP myosin cannot detach from actin, so the muscles lock. That begins around 3 hours. The stiffness fades by about 72 hours not because ATP returns but because the muscle proteins themselves begin to break down. It is the reason time of death can be estimated from rigidity.

Source: the lecture's fatigue versus rigor mortis slide.

deeper.title: Why Duchenne boys push up on their thighs
deeper.html:
Duchenne weakens the proximal muscles of the hips and shoulders first. Standing from the floor needs strong hip extensors, so the child walks his hands up his own legs to push his trunk upright, a manoeuvre called Gowers' sign. The calves look big not from strength but because muscle is being replaced by fat and fibrous tissue.

Source: the lecture's Duchenne clinical case.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Covasa's lecture: motor activity and reflexes, the myotatic reflex and its tonic and phasic phases, its clinical exploration and the H-reflex, the muscle spindle and its afferents and efferents, reciprocal inhibition, the other spinal reflexes and the clinical signs. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Reflex location sets which muscle contracts; strength sets the amplitude.
Myotatic reflex: monosynaptic, triggered by sudden passive stretch; agonist contracts, antagonist relaxes.
Tonic phase maintains posture; phasic phase uses Ia afferents.
Hyporeflexia: lesion of the arc. Hyperreflexia: suprasegmental lesion.
Grades 0 to 4+; 2+ is normal.
Patellar: quadriceps. Achilles: soleus. Bicipital: biceps. Tricipital: triceps.
H-reflex: M wave first, H wave later.
Spindle signals length (in parallel); Golgi tendon organ signals tension (Ib).
Spindle: four to eight intrafusal fibres, nuclear chain and nuclear bag.
Ia: length and speed, 70 to 110 m/s. II: length only, 30 to 70 m/s.
Reciprocal inhibition relaxes the antagonist through an inhibitory interneuron.
Gamma motor neurons keep the spindle sensitive; alpha-gamma coactivation.
Patellar centre L2 to L4.
Babinski after 1.5 years indicates a corticospinal lesion.

deeper.title: Why a stroke makes reflexes brisk
deeper.html:
The spinal reflex arc is normally held in check by descending pathways from the brain, which damp the motor neurons. A stroke or spinal cord injury above the reflex level removes that brake, so the arc overreacts: brisk reflexes, clonus and a positive Babinski sign. That is why the lecture links hyperreflexia to a suprasegmental lesion.

Source: the lecture's homeostatic imbalance slides.

deeper.title: Why diabetes abolishes ankle reflexes first
deeper.html:
Diabetic neuropathy damages the longest nerve fibres first, and the fibres to and from the calf are among the longest in the body. The Ia afferents of the Achilles reflex fail before those of the shorter patellar reflex, so a missing ankle jerk is often an early sign of diabetic nerve damage.

Source: the lecture's Achilles and patellar reflex clinical notes.

deeper.title: Why the spindle needs its own motor supply
deeper.html:
Without gamma motor neurons, a contracting muscle would go slack around its spindles, which would stop signalling just when the brain most needs to know the muscle's length. Alpha-gamma coactivation shortens the spindle along with the muscle, keeping it taut and informative throughout the movement.

Source: the lecture's gamma efferent and coactivation slides.

deeper.title: Why babies have a positive Babinski sign
deeper.html:
The corticospinal tract is not fully myelinated in infants, so the adult pattern of curling the toes down is not yet imposed on the spinal reflex. The primitive extensor response shows through. Once the tract matures, around 1.5 years, a positive Babinski means the tract has been damaged.

Source: the lecture's Babinski sign slide.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. This page follows Prof. Covasa's lecture: nervous system cells and the structure of the neuron, ion channels, the resting membrane potential, graded and action potentials, and conduction velocity. Every fact was cross-checked against at least two references, listed at the bottom. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Neurons signal; neuroglia (ependymal cells, astrocytes, Schwann cells, oligodendrocytes, microglia) support.
Four zones: input (dendrites, soma), trigger (axon hillock), conducting (axon), output (terminals).
One axon per neuron; no centrosome, so no division.
Nissl granules absent from the axon and axon hillock.
Channels: mechanical, voltage, ligand, phosphorylation-gated and leak. Flux is always passive.
Resting potential -70 mV; K+ equilibrium -90 mV; Na+ equilibrium +60 mV.
At rest K+ leak channels are open, so the potential sits near the K+ equilibrium.
Graded potentials vary with stimulus and fade; action potentials are all or none.
Threshold about -50 to -55 mV.
Rising phase: Na+ in. Falling phase: K+ out. Dip: slow K+ channels close late.
Na+ channels inactivate by a separate gate, making propagation one-way.
Conduction velocity rises with myelination and diameter: up to 120 m/s.
Saltatory conduction: node to node, at the nodes of Ranvier.

deeper.title: Why demyelination slows or blocks the nerve
deeper.html:
In a myelinated axon the voltage-gated channels sit almost only at the nodes of Ranvier. Strip the myelin away and the current leaks out across a membrane with too few channels to regenerate it, so conduction slows or fails entirely. That is the mechanism of multiple sclerosis in the CNS and of some neuropathies in the PNS, and it follows directly from how saltatory conduction works.

Source: the lecture's myelination and saltatory conduction slides.

deeper.title: Why local anaesthetics stop pain
deeper.html:
Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated Na+ channels. With no Na+ rushing in, the rising phase can never happen, so no action potential forms and the pain signal never leaves the area. Small, unmyelinated pain fibres are blocked first, which is why pain goes before touch and movement.

Source: the lecture's voltage-gated Na+ channel and axon diameter slides.

deeper.title: Why potassium levels matter so much clinically
deeper.html:
The resting potential sits near the K+ equilibrium because K+ leak channels dominate at rest. Change the potassium concentration outside the cell and the resting potential moves with it. High potassium depolarises cells toward threshold, which is why dangerous potassium levels can disturb the heart's rhythm.

Source: the lecture's resting potential and forces on ion movement slides.

deeper.title: Why a stronger stimulus fires more often, not bigger
deeper.html:
Because the action potential is all or none, a neuron cannot signal a stronger stimulus by making its spikes bigger. Instead a stronger stimulus reaches threshold faster after each spike, so the neuron fires more often. Intensity is coded in frequency, not amplitude.

Source: the lecture's graded potential versus action potential slides.

figure.caption: The phases of a neuronal action potential. The dashed line marks threshold. Schematic, not to scale.

exam_points: Pain: unpleasant sensory and emotional experience; nociception: unconscious activity.
Hyperalgesia: exaggerated; allodynia: pain from harmless stimuli.
Fast pain: A-delta, 6 to 30 m/s, glutamate, lamina I, neospinothalamic.
Slow pain: C, 0.5 to 2 m/s, glutamate + substance P, laminae II and III, paleospinothalamic.
Pain receptors are free nerve endings and barely adapt.

Referred pain: shared second-order neurons.
Liver, alveoli and brain are almost insensitive.

deeper.title: Why heart attack pain is felt in the left arm
deeper.html:
Cardiac pain fibres enter the same upper thoracic cord segments as skin fibres from the chest wall and inner left arm, and synapse on the same second-order neurons. The brain, used to signals from skin, reads the pain as coming from the arm. That is referred pain, and it is why arm pain can be the only warning of a heart attack.

Source: the lecture's referred pain mechanism slide.

deeper.title: Why aspirin-type drugs reduce inflammatory pain
deeper.html:
Prostaglandin E2, made by cyclooxygenase, does not excite pain endings itself but sensitises them to everything else. Drugs that block cyclooxygenase remove that sensitisation, so the same injury hurts less. It follows from the lecture's distinction between exciters and sensitisers.

Source: the lecture's chemical mediator slides.

deeper.html: Because pH depends on the HCO3−/PCO2 ratio, a primary change in one is partly compensated by the other: a metabolic acidosis (HCO3− ↓) is followed by hyperventilation (PCO2 ↓), and a respiratory acidosis (PCO2 ↑) by renal HCO3− retention over days. Beyond the lecture.

exam_points: GFR about 125 mL/min (men), 105 (women); about 180 L/day.
99 percent of filtrate reabsorbed; urine 1 to 2 L/day.
Barrier: fenestrated endothelium (70 to 90 nm), basement membrane (negative, excludes over 8 nm), podocyte slits (30 nm).
Molecules under 3 nm pass freely; protein-bound Ca, Fe, thyroid hormone do not.
Proteinuria and haematuria from filter damage.

deeper.title: Why protein in the urine points to kidney damage
deeper.html:
The basement membrane and podocyte slits are negatively charged, repelling negatively charged albumin. When disease disrupts these layers, albumin leaks through, which is why proteinuria is one of the earliest and most important signs of glomerular damage, for example in diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease.

Source: the lecture's filtration barrier slides.

deeper.title: Why dehydration can make the kidneys fail
deeper.html:
Filtration depends on a net pressure of only about 10 mmHg. A fall in blood pressure from dehydration or bleeding cuts glomerular pressure, GFR falls, and wastes accumulate: azotemia. The kidneys defend GFR by adjusting their arterioles, but only up to a point.

Source: the lecture's filtration pressure and GFR regulation slides, with textbook values.

provenance.note: Renal Physiology 4 (Regulation of GFR).pdf (Kidney Physiology, lecture 4, S3, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: GFR control: autoregulation, sympathetic, hormonal.
Autoregulation works without nerves or hormones: myogenic (intrinsic) and tubuloglomerular feedback (extrinsic).
Myogenic = Bayliss effect: stretch → afferent constriction; low pressure → afferent dilation.
Macula densa = NaCl chemoreceptor; granular cells = BP mechanoreceptors containing renin.
High GFR → more NaCl → ATP → adenosine → afferent constriction → GFR ↓.
Renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I; ACE (lungs, kidney) → angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II: vasoconstriction, efferent constriction, aldosterone, ADH, thirst, PCT Na+ reabsorption.
ANP/BNP: afferent dilation, efferent constriction, GFR ↑, natriuresis, renin and aldosterone ↓.

deeper.title: ACE inhibitors and the efferent arteriole
deeper.html: Because angiotensin II holds the efferent arteriole tight, blocking it (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) lowers glomerular pressure. That protects kidneys in diabetes but can drop GFR sharply in renal artery stenosis. Beyond the lecture.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Kidneys: retroperitoneal; ureters transport, bladder stores, urethra carries out.
Filter plasma: metabolic wastes, hormones, drugs and toxins, free radicals.
Urea: amino acids → ammonia → urea in the liver. Uric acid: nucleic acids. Creatinine: creatine phosphate.
Albuminuria, proteinuria, glucosuria, acetonuria (ketones), haematuria (RBC), pyuria (WBC).
Blood homeostasis: volume, pressure, osmolarity, electrolytes, acid-base.
EPO: up to more than 100-fold in hypoxia; HIF senses low O2 (Nobel 2019).
Calcitriol (vitamin D) synthesis helps regulate calcium.
Gluconeogenesis from amino acids in starvation.

deeper.title: Why EPO rises in kidney failure patients is a problem
deeper.html: In chronic kidney disease the cells that make EPO are lost, so patients become anaemic even though the hypoxia signal is present. This is why recombinant EPO (and more recently HIF-stabilising drugs) are used in renal anaemia. Beyond the lecture.

provenance.note: Renal Physiology 2 (Physiology of the nephron).pdf (Kidney Physiology, lecture 2, S3, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Nephron = glomerulus + renal tubule; over 1 million per kidney; lose about 1% per year after 30.
Afferent arteriole larger than efferent; fenestrated capillaries; podocytes, pedicels, filtration slits.
Mesangial cells contract to regulate flow and engulf trapped macromolecules.
Four processes: filtration, reabsorption, secretion, water conservation.
GFR 2 mL/s, 120 mL/min, about 170 L/day; 20% of plasma is filtered.
Reabsorbed 119 mL/min; urine 1 mL/min, about 1.5 L/day.
ADH → receptor → cAMP → AQP2 into apical membrane → water by osmosis.
ADH max: urine 0.25 mL/min (375 mL/day); no ADH: 15 mL/min (22.5 L/day).

deeper.title: Diabetes insipidus
deeper.html: When ADH is missing (central) or the collecting duct cannot respond (nephrogenic), urine approaches the 'no ADH' figures of the lecture: many litres a day of dilute urine with intense thirst. Beyond the lecture.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Cortical nephrons 85% (short loops, peritubular capillaries); juxtamedullary 15% (long loops, vasa recta, concentrate urine).
Transcellular and paracellular (leaky junctions) routes; peritubular capillaries take up the fluid.
Basal Na+–K+ pump = primary active; apical symports = secondary active.
Glucose: SGLT with Na+; normally all reabsorbed.
PCT: 65% of filtrate; microvilli, mitochondria; 6% of resting ATP; fluid leaves isosmotic.
Descending limb: 20% more water, unregulated. Final 15%: hormonal.
Descending limb permeable to water only; ascending limb to solutes only.
Countercurrent multiplier builds 300 → about 1 200-1 400 mOsm.

deeper.title: SGLT2 inhibitors
deeper.html: Drugs such as dapagliflozin block SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, so glucose escapes into the urine: a way to lower blood glucose in type 2 diabetes that also protects heart and kidney. Beyond the lecture.

provenance.note: Covasa Physiology of Stress.pdf (Neurophysiology, Prof. Mihai Covasa, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides, including your professor's own review questions. Slides marked FYI are covered only in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Stressor challenges homeostasis; stress is the response.
Resilience: bouncing back. Hardiness: staying healthy.
Selye 1936: general adaptation syndrome; triad of adrenal enlargement, lymphoid involution, gastric ulcers.
Fast phase SN and SAM; slow phase HPA.
Acute stress: under 2 days to 4 weeks; chronic: over a month.
Fight or flight: GI blood flow falls; cardiac output, glucose and epinephrine rise.
HPA: CRH (PVN), ACTH (anterior pituitary), cortisol (adrenal cortex).
Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH.
Glomerulosa aldosterone; fasciculata cortisol; medulla catecholamines.
Locus coeruleus noradrenaline; raphe serotonin.
Hippocampus to PVN ends the response.
Prolonged stress lowers GH and prolactin.

deeper.title: Why chronic stress can shrink the hippocampus
deeper.html:
The hippocampus is the brake on the HPA axis, but it is also full of cortisol receptors. Sustained high cortisol damages it, which weakens the brake, which keeps cortisol high. The lecture describes exactly this vicious circle, and it helps explain the memory problems seen with long-term stress and depression.

Source: the lecture's termination of stress slide.

deeper.title: Why stress can cause stomach ulcers
deeper.html:
Selye found bleeding ulcers in stressed animals, and the lecture lists acid and pepsin hypersecretion in chronic stress. Add the fight-or-flight drop in gut blood flow, which weakens the mucosa's defences, and the stomach lining is attacked while poorly protected.

Source: the lecture's general adaptation syndrome and chronic stress slides.

provenance.note: Covasa Taste & Olfaction lecture.pdf (Neurophysiology, Prof. Mihai Covasa, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Several slides, including the olfactory transduction diagrams, are images only; their content was filled in from the listed references. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Five tastes: salty, sweet, sour, bitter, umami (fat possible).
Sour and bitter innately aversive; responses innate in newborns.
About 100 receptor cells per taste bud.
Tastants must dissolve in saliva; Ca2+ influx releases transmitter.
Salty: amiloride-sensitive Na+ channel; sour: PKD2L1.
Ageusia = taste loss; anosmia = smell loss.
Olfactory receptors are neurons; smells habituate quickly.
Parosmia distorted; phantosmia without odour; cacosmia all unpleasant.
New bulb neurons from the subventricular zone.
Smell loss: early sign of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.

deeper.title: Why food tastes bland with a cold
deeper.html:
The lecture stresses that taste perception depends heavily on smell. With a blocked nose, odour molecules from food cannot reach the olfactory neurons, so only the five basic tastes remain, and most of what we call flavour disappears.

Source: the lecture's perception of taste slide.

deeper.title: Why a smell test can help diagnose Parkinson's
deeper.html:
Olfactory loss often appears years before the tremor and stiffness of Parkinson's disease or the memory loss of Alzheimer's. Because it is cheap to test, a new unexplained loss of smell in an older adult can be an early clue worth following up.

Source: the lecture's key messages slide.

provenance.note: Covasa Vestibular System 2025.pdf (Neurophysiology, Prof. M. Covasa, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Otolith organs: linear acceleration and gravity; canals: angular acceleration.
Cupula in canals; otolithic membrane in maculae.
Bending toward the tallest stereocilium depolarises.
Utricle horizontal, saccule vertical.
Start of rotation: crista tilts opposite; stop: same way; steady: rest.
Turning right excites the right lateral canal.
Superior division: lateral and anterior cristae, utricle; inferior: saccule, posterior crista.
Vestibular nerve enters at the cerebellopontine angle.
MLF links vestibular nuclei to III, IV, VI.
Caloric test: lateral canal; MLF lesion: internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

deeper.title: Why you feel dizzy after spinning then stopping
deeper.html:
During steady spinning the endolymph catches up and the cupula rests. When you stop suddenly, the endolymph keeps moving and bends the cupula the other way, so the canal signals rotation in the opposite direction even though you are still. Your eyes jerk (nystagmus) and the room seems to spin until the fluid settles.

Source: the lecture's crista ampullaris slides.

deeper.title: Why motion sickness makes you nauseous
deeper.html:
The lecture notes that vestibular input reaches the vagal reflex pathway, which is why Ménière's disease causes nausea. When vestibular signals disagree with what the eyes report, as below deck on a boat, the same pathway can trigger nausea and vomiting.

Source: the lecture's Ménière's disease and integration slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Visible light: purple to red.
Dioptre = 1 / focal length (m).
Four refraction points; cornea holds two thirds of power.
Corneal reflex: V in, VII out.
Light reflex: pretectal, Edinger-Westphal, ciliary ganglion; direct and consensual.
Aqueous: ciliary body to canal of Schlemm; blockage causes glaucoma.
Ciliary contraction thickens the lens for near vision.
Near response: accommodation, miosis, convergence.
Myopia in front, hyperopia behind; presbyopia from a stiff lens.
Normal acuity 20/20.
Fovea: highest acuity; optic disc: blind spot.
Rods scotopic; cones photopic and colour.
Only ganglion cells fire action potentials.

deeper.title: Why pupil checks are part of every head injury exam
deeper.html:
The light reflex runs through the midbrain, right beside the brainstem's vital centres. A pupil that stops reacting after head trauma can mean swelling is pressing on the brainstem or on CN III, which is why doctors shine a light in the eyes of every injured patient.

Source: the lecture's light reflex slides.

deeper.title: Why reading glasses arrive in your forties
deeper.html:
Near vision needs the lens to round up when the ciliary muscle contracts. As lens proteins denature with age, the lens stiffens and can no longer round up enough, so near objects blur even though distance vision is fine. That is presbyopia, and convex reading lenses supply the missing power.

Source: the lecture's accommodation and presbyopia slides.
